app.title: Merrypopins: Nano-indentation Pop-in Detector
app.summary: A person uploads one indentation test file, with an optional metadata file, and checks its first rows, point count and load range. They choose how to preprocess the load–depth curve and compare the raw and preprocessed curves on one plot, with the contact point marked. Next they set and turn on any of four event detectors and run them. A summary shows how many events each method found and how many at least two methods agreed on, and the flags are drawn over the curve. Then the app computes statistics for each event: depth jump and duration, and stress–strain jumps and slopes. Each table and plot can be downloaded, and a ZIP bundles the results with the settings used.

task.text: Detect sudden discontinuities in an indentation load–depth curve with several detectors, keep the ones the detectors agree on, and compute statistics for each event to export.

data.text: Raw instrument output from one test: a load, depth and time curve sampled point by point, with optional channel metadata. The app adds a per-point flag from each detector and builds a table with one row per event.
data.item: one indentation test: a load–depth–time curve, and the events detected along it

stage.text: analysing raw indentation curves right after testing, from cleaning the curve to per-event statistics

mechanism.text: Settings in the sidebar control preprocessing, edge trimming and statistics, and the main page reruns from top to bottom: a file preview, an overlay of the raw and preprocessed curves, a panel of four detectors, a count of detections with flagged points drawn over the curve, and statistics tables with scatter plots. Each stage has its own CSV and PNG downloads.

field.text: pop-in detection in nanoindentation load–depth curves, in materials science

workflow.name: flag events in a signal with several detectors and compute statistics for each event

steps.here: Upload an indentation .txt file, plus an optional .tdm/.tdx metadata file. The app shows the first rows, the point count, the minimum and maximum load, the timestamp, and the metadata channels.

steps.step: clean the signal before computing on it
steps.here: Choose Default, Custom or None preprocessing. Custom options remove points before the minimum load, rescale depth from a baseline noise threshold, and trim or flag the contact point. The raw and preprocessed curves are overlaid, with the contact point circled.

steps.step: compute a value from the data
steps.here: Turn on and tune Isolation Forest, CNN autoencoder, Fourier-derivative and Savitzky–Golay detectors, then click 'Run selected detectors'. Each detector flags points, and those flags are combined into an any-method flag and a count of how many methods agree.

steps.step: compare methods on the same items
steps.here: Metrics show total pop-ins, the number flagged by at least two methods, and each method's hits. A load–depth plot marks each method's detections in its own colour, and the agreed detections in black.

Using time windows before and after each event, the app computes depth jump and pop-in length, then stress and strain jumps and slopes, plus the full stress–strain series. Each result has a table and a scatter plot. Rows with all values missing can be dropped.

Download the preprocessed CSV, the annotated detections CSV, each statistics CSV and every plot as PNG. A ZIP bundles the annotated CSV, the detections plot and the preprocessing and trim settings as JSON.

distinctive: Four different detectors (an isolation forest, a CNN autoencoder, a Fourier derivative and a Savitzky–Golay derivative) run on the same curve. A point counts as a confident event when at least two of them flag it.
The contact point is found and flagged during preprocessing. Edge trimming can drop the first points and everything after maximum load before detection.
Events are turned into stress–strain jumps and slopes using a fixed effective indenter radius and a minimum load threshold, with optional stress smoothing.
The ZIP saves the preprocessing and trimming settings alongside the results so a run can be reproduced.
